claim: The Ai14D reporter mouse strain carries a transgene at the Rosa26 locus with a ubiquitously expressed CAG promoter driving expression of a transgene with a 3× STOP cassette flanked by two LoxP sites, followed by a fluorescent reporter gene encoding tdTomato.
source: This reporter carries a transgene at the 'safe harbor' Rosa26 locus, with a ubiquitously expressed CAG promoter driving expression of a transgene with a 3× STOP cassette flanked by two LoxP sites, followed by a fluorescent reporter gene encoding tdTomato.
evidence: The manuscript describes the genetic construct of the Ai14D reporter strain, which is a well-characterized tool referenced in the methods.

claim: Cre recombinase excises the STOP cassette in the Ai14D reporter, resulting in robust tdTomato expression in Cre-expressing cells.
source: Cre recombinase excises the STOP cassette, resulting in robust tdTomato (hereafter, Tomato) expression in Cre-expressing cells.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the Cre-Lox system used in the study, which is established knowledge and demonstrated in the experiments.

claim: Defb41iCre drives reporter expression in a highly localized manner in the proximal (caput) epididymis.
source: Consistent with the distribution of Defb41 mRNA expression observed in surveys of epididymal gene expression (Johnston et al., 2005; Rinaldi et al., 2020), we find that Defb41iCre drives reporter expression in a highly localized manner in the proximal (caput) epididymis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with cited literature on Defb41 expression patterns.

claim: Tomato expression driven by Defb41iCre is confined to the principal cells of the epididymal epithelium.
source: cross sections show that Tomato expression is confined to the principal cells (but not basal or other interstitial cells) of the epididymal epithelium (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through histological analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Tomato expression driven by Defb41iCre is notably absent from the sperm-filled lumen.
source: Tomato expression is notably absent from the sperm-filled lumen.
evidence: This observation is made from the imaging data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Stereotaxic delivery of AAV constructs engineered to drive Cre expression in the mouse brain results in robust Tomato expression in the cauda epididymis and vas deferens.
source: Remarkably, examination of the epididymis in both cases revealed robust Tomato expression in the cauda (distal) epididymis and in the vas deferens (Figure 2C).
evidence: This finding is demonstrated through experimental data from AAV injection experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Tomato expression was reproducibly observed in all epididymis samples isolated from ten AAV-transduced animals.
source: Tomato expression was reproducibly observed in all epididymis samples isolated from ten AAV-transduced animals, including three animals injected in the prefrontal cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) as well as seven animals injected in the lateral somatosensory cortex, caudate putamen, and nucleus accumbens (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data on the number of animals showing the effect.

claim: Tomato expression following AAV-induced Cre expression was confined to the epididymal epithelium with no detectable expression in the sperm filling the epididymal lumen.
source: As in the case of the Defb41iCre driver, closer examination of our imaging data showed that Tomato expression was confined to the epididymal epithelium (inset, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), with no detectable expression in the sperm filling the epididymal lumen (see below).
evidence: This is based on microscopic examination of the tissue samples shown in the figures.

claim: Cre expression from the Slc32a1 transgene resulted in robust epididymal Tomato expression in Ai14D; Slc32a1Cre double transgenic animals.
source: Remarkably, similar to the reporter expression observed following viral induction of neuronal Cre expression (Figure 2), Cre expression from the Slc32a1 transgene also resulted in robust epididymal Tomato expression in Ai14D; Slc32a1Cre double transgenic animals (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Microscopy revealed Tomato expression exclusively in the principal cells of the epididymal epithelium in Ai14D; Slc32a1Cre animals.
source: Closer inspection of double transgenic epididymis by microscopy revealed Tomato expression exclusively in the principal cells of the epididymal epithelium (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The presence of Tomato-positive principal cells in Ai14D; Slc32a1Cre animals was confirmed by FACS.
source: and we further confirmed the presence of Tomato-positive principal cells by FACS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Patchy Tomato expression was observed in histological cross sections of Ai14D; Slc32a1Cre epididymis.
source: Intriguingly, we observed patchy Tomato expression in any given histological cross section
evidence: This observation is made from histological analysis of the tissue.

claim: Recombination at the reporter locus was detected in genomic DNA isolated from the epididymis of Ai14D; Slc32a1Cre animals.
source: We therefore assayed recombination at the LoxP-STOP cassette in the epididymis, finding recombination at the reporter locus in genomic DNA isolated from the epididymis (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PCR analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The findings strongly support the hypothesis that Cre activity (RNA or protein) is the relevant molecular signal trafficked from the CNS to the epididymis.
source: These findings strongly support the hypothesis that Cre activity (RNA or protein) is the relevant molecular signal trafficked from the CNS to the epididymis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing recombination at the reporter locus.

claim: A wide range of neuronal Cre lines drive Tomato expression in the epididymis.
source: Most notably, we find that a wide range of neuronal Cre lines drive Tomato expression in the epididymis.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from multiple Cre driver lines tested in the study.

claim: Extensive Tomato staining was found throughout the epididymis in both Synapsin and Nestin Cre double transgenic lines.
source: Focusing first on the putative 'pan-neuronal' Cre lines, driven by the Synapsin or Nestin promoters, we found extensive Tomato staining throughout the epididymis in both double transgenic lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Tomato expression in Ai14D; SynCre animals was not limited to the epididymal epithelium and instead filled the epididymis lumen, suggestive of Tomato-positive sperm.
source: However, we noted that Tomato expression in the SynCre animals was not limited to the epididymal epithelium and instead filled the epididymis lumen (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), suggestive of Tomato-positive sperm.
evidence: This observation is made from imaging data and is consistent with germline recombination.

claim: Offspring of Ai14D; SynCre double transgenics exhibited Tomato expression throughout the body, consistent with prior reports of SynCre driving germline recombination.
source: Indeed, offspring of the Ai14D; SynCre double transgenics exhibited Tomato expression throughout the body, consistent with prior reports of SynCre driving germline recombination (Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and is supported by cited literature.

claim: The Nestin Cre driver has been reported to drive germline recombination.
source: Similarly, the Nestin Cre driver has also been reported to drive germline recombination (Betz et al., 1996; McLeod et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tomato-positive offspring were obtained from Ai14D; NesCre double transgenics.
source: and we did obtain Tomato-positive offspring of Ai14D; NesCre double transgenics.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: In contrast to Ai14D; SynCre animals, no detectable labeling of sperm was found in Ai14D; NesCre animals, with Tomato expression in the epididymis largely confined to the epididymal epithelium.
source: That said, in contrast to the Ai14D; SynCre animals we found no detectable labeling of sperm in Ai14D; NesCre animals, with Tomato expression in the epididymis largely confined to the epididymal epithelium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: NesCre-mediated recombination likely occurs relatively late during spermatogenesis in germ cells, with recombination in the epididymal epithelium occurring independently.
source: This suggests that NesCre-mediated recombination occurs relatively late during spermatogenesis in germ cells, with recombination in the epididymal epithelium occurring independently – probably induced by the same CNS→epididymis trafficking seen for several other neuronal Cre drivers (Figure 3 and below).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of Tomato expression observed.

claim: Tomato expression was consistently observed in the epididymis when Cre was expressed from Slc32a1, Fev, Gad2, and Drd1a promoters.
source: Turning from pan-neuronal promoters to more cell type-specific CNS Cre drivers, we consistently observed Tomato expression in the epididymis when Cre was expressed from Slc32a1, Fev, Gad2, and Drd1a promoters (Figures 3–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: For Fev and Slc32a1 Cre drivers, Tomato expression was strongest in the cauda epididymis and vas deferens.
source: For two of these Cre drivers – Fev and Slc32a1 – we find that Tomato expression was strongest in the cauda epididymis and vas deferens, similar to our findings obtained using AAV to drive Cre expression in the CNS.
evidence: This is based on imaging data comparing different Cre drivers.

claim: Both Ai14D; Gad2Cre and Ai14D; Drd1aCre double transgenic animals exhibited patchy epithelial staining throughout the epididymis.
source: In contrast, both Ai14D; Gad2Cre and Ai14D; Drd1aCre double transgenic animals exhibited patchy epithelial staining throughout the epididymis (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Off-target epididymal recombination was not unique to neuronal Cre drivers, as robust Tomato expression and reporter locus recombination was observed in animals carrying the adipose-specific AdipoqCre.
source: Intriguingly, off-target epididymal recombination was not unique to neuronal Cre drivers, as we also observed robust Tomato expression and reporter locus recombination in animals carrying the adipose-specific AdipoqCre (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Reporter animals carrying the liver-specific AlbCre transgene exhibited barely detectable Tomato expression in the epididymis with few Tomato-positive cells detected throughout the entire tissue.
source: In contrast, reporter animals carrying the liver-specific AlbCre transgene exhibited barely detectable Tomato expression in the epididymis with few Tomato-positive cells detected throughout the entire tissue – at most one or two cells per longitudinal section (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Multiple neuronal Cre drivers exhibited off-target activities in tissues beyond the epididymis, most notably in the reproductive accessory glands.
source: Not only did non-neuronal Cre drivers direct recombination in the epididymis, but multiple neuronal Cre drivers exhibited off-target activities in tissues beyond the epididymis. Most notably, within the male reproductive tract we observed robust Tomato expression in the reproductive accessory glands of the Nes, Fev, and Gad2 lines (Figure 4—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: Publicly available annotations from MGI show clear evidence for recombination in the epididymis epithelium for Syn1Cre.
source: Of the lines that drive recombination in Ai14D in our study, there is also clear evidence for recombination in the epididymis epithelium for Syn1Cre
evidence: This is based on examination of publicly available data from MGI.

claim: MGI annotations show 'ambiguous' expression for NesCre and Gad2Cre in the epididymis.
source: along with 'ambiguous' expression annotated for NesCre and Gad2Cre.
evidence: This is based on examination of publicly available data from MGI.

claim: Closer examination of the MGI image provided for NesCre revealed clear evidence for reporter expression in the epididymis epithelium.
source: However, closer examination of the image provided for NesCre also revealed clear evidence for reporter expression in the epididymis epithelium
evidence: This is based on examination of publicly available images from MGI.

claim: Adipoq, Slc32a1, Drd1, and Fev were all annotated as 'absent' in the epididymis epithelium in MGI at postnatal days 7 and 56.
source: Conversely, Adipoq, Slc32a1, Drd1, and Fev were all annotated as 'absent' in the epididymis epithelium (at postnatal days 7 and 56).
evidence: This is based on examination of publicly available data from MGI.

claim: Recombination of the Dicer1 locus was confirmed specifically in the cauda epididymis of AdipoqCre; Dicer1flx/flx animals.
source: Using this assay, we document recombination of this locus specifically in the cauda epididymis, but not in the testis or other parts of the epididymis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PCR genotyping shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Off-target recombination in the epididymis is not unique to the Ai14D reporter.
source: These data thus extend our results to a second target locus, demonstrating that off-target recombination in the epididymis is not unique to the Ai14D reporter.
evidence: This is based on experimental data using the Dicer1 conditional allele.

claim: Moderate Tomato expression was detected in the epididymis of the Ai14D recipient animal in a parabiotic Ai14D::Slc32a1Cre pair.
source: We detected moderate Tomato expression in the epididymis of the Ai14D recipient animal in a parabiotic Ai14D:: Slc32a1Cre pair (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is demonstrated through histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: A faint band supporting recombination at the reporter locus was detected in one Ai14D recipient from parabiosis.
source: along with a faint band supporting recombination at the reporter locus in one recipient (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PCR analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In two other Ai14D animals from parabiosis, no evidence for recombination was found by PCR.
source: However, in two other Ai14D animals we found no evidence for recombination by PCR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is demonstrated through PCR analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Serum transfer from Slc32a1Cre animals to Ai14D males resulted in epididymal LoxP recombination and Tomato expression.
source: As shown in Figure 6E–F, this resulted in epididymal LoxP recombination and Tomato expression in animals receiving Slc32a1Cre serum
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging and PCR analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Recipients of serum from FVB or AlbCre animals did not express Tomato or exhibit recombination at the reporter locus.
source: while recipients of serum from FVB or AlbCre animals did not express Tomato or exhibit recombination at the reporter locus.
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging and PCR analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: No Tomato expression was found in an Ai14D male that had received TFF-enriched exosomes from nine Slc32a1Cre animals spread across 3 injection days.
source: We found no Tomato expression in an Ai14D male that had received TFF-enriched exosomes from nine Slc32a1Cre animals spread across 3 injection days (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, top right panel).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Across over 20 recipient animals in serum/exosome transfer experiments, clear evidence for recombination was documented in six animals.
source: Ultimately, across over 20 recipient animals we documented clear evidence for recombination in six animals, with positive results in recipients of Slc32a1Cre serum, Slc32a1Cre serum and exosomes, Gad2Cre serum and exosomes, a mixture of Gad2Cre and Drd1Cre serum and exosomes, NesCre serum and exosomes, and AdipoqCre serum and exosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from multiple serum/exosome transfer experiments.

claim: Similar or nearly identical injection schemes in serum/exosome transfer experiments often resulted in no detectable Tomato expression or recombination.
source: However, similar or nearly identical injection schemes often resulted in no detectable Tomato expression or recombination.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations across multiple trials.

claim: The data support the hypothesis that off-target Cre activity in the epididymis is likely mediated by Cre trafficking through the circulation.
source: Taken together, our data support the hypothesis that off-target Cre activity in the epididymis is likely mediated by Cre trafficking through the circulation
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the parabiosis and serum transfer experimental data.

claim: The difficulty in reliably replicating Cre transfer impedes further mechanistic follow-up.
source: although the difficulty in reliably replicating this transfer impedes further mechanistic follow-up.
evidence: This is based on the experimental challenges encountered in the serum/exosome transfer studies.

claim: The epididymis is a surprisingly common 'off-target' tissue for a variety of Cre drivers that are not believed to be expressed in the male reproductive tract.
source: Our observations reveal the epididymis as a surprisingly common 'off-target' tissue for a variety of Cre drivers that are not believed to be expressed in the male reproductive tract.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from multiple Cre driver lines.

claim: There is a many-to-many mapping between sender tissues and recipient tissues, with sender tissues including multiple neuronal subpopulations along with adipose tissue, and recipient tissues including the epididymis, seminal vesicle, prostate, and intestine.
source: We find a many-to-many mapping, with 'sender' tissues including multiple neuronal subpopulations along with adipose tissue, and recipient tissues including the epididymis, seminal vesicle, prostate, and intestine.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings across multiple Cre driver lines and tissues examined.

claim: Different Cre lines drive recombination in different sets of tissues, arguing against the possibility that a generic 'sink' tissue nonspecifically receives any RNAs or proteins present in the circulation.
source: Importantly, different Cre lines drive recombination in different sets of tissues, arguing against the possibility that a generic 'sink' tissue nonspecifically receives any RNAs or proteins present in the circulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential patterns of recombination observed with different Cre drivers.

claim: The data confirm prior reports of germline activity of NesCre and Syn1Cre drivers.
source: and here for example our data confirm prior reports of germline activity of NesCre and Syn1Cre drivers (Luo et al., 2020; Betz et al., 1996; McLeod et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations that are consistent with cited literature.

claim: The findings identify many new examples of off-target Cre activity for a variety of Cre lines.
source: Our findings also identify many new examples of off-target Cre activity for a variety of Cre lines
evidence: This is based on the novel experimental findings reported in the study.

claim: Many off-target Cre activities may have been missed before given the relatively small size of the scientific community focused on the epididymis.
source: many of which may have been missed before given the relatively small size of the scientific community focused on the epididymis.
evidence: This is speculation about why these off-target effects were not previously reported.

claim: Fairly patchy recombination was found in the epididymal epithelium even in cases of double transgenics exhibiting robust recombination.
source: It is worth noting that even in the cases of double transgenics exhibiting robust recombination in the epididymis (Slc32a1, Adipoq, etc. – Figures 3—5), we find fairly patchy recombination in the epididymal epithelium.
evidence: This is based on histological observations from the imaging data.

claim: The data showing off-target Cre activity in the epididymis are unlikely to result from leaky expression of the Cre drivers studied.
source: That said, our data showing off-target Cre activity in the epididymis are unlikely to result from leaky expression of the Cre drivers studied here, for multiple reasons.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: Most of the neuron-specific genes in question are not detectably expressed in the adult epididymis.
source: First of all, we find a wide range of Cre transgenes drive recombination in the epididymis, and most of the neuron-specific genes in question are not detectably expressed in the adult epididymis (Johnston et al., 2005; Rinaldi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on epididymal gene expression.

claim: Induction of Cre expression in the brain via AAV-mediated transduction leads to reporter activity in the epididymis epithelium, which cannot be explained by leaky transgene expression.
source: However, our observation that induction of Cre expression in the brain via AAV-mediated transduction leads to reporter activity in the epididymis epithelium (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2) cannot be explained by leaky transgene expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the AAV injection experimental data.

claim: The findings strongly suggest that Cre activity synthesized in neurons is transported to the epididymis.
source: Together, these findings strongly suggest that Cre activity synthesized in neurons is transported to the epididymis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined evidence from AAV and transgenic experiments.

claim: Delivery of Cre from neurons to the epididymis via release of Cre-containing vesicles by peripheral neurons that innervate the cauda epididymis is considered unlikely.
source: The delivery of Cre from neurons to the epididymis could occur via a number of routes, including release of Cre-containing vesicles by peripheral neurons that innervate the cauda epididymis. We consider this to be unlikely for several reasons.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on multiple lines of evidence discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Adipose-specific Cre expression reliably drives recombination in the epididymis, arguing against Cre transfer requiring neuronal termini.
source: First, we show that adipose-specific Cre expression reliably drives recombination in the epididymis (Figure 5), arguing against Cre transfer requiring neuronal termini.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data from AdipoqCre animals.

claim: Induction of Cre expression specifically in one hemisphere of the brain via stereotactic AAV injections led to Tomato expression in both the ipsilateral and contralateral epididymis.
source: Second, induction of Cre expression specifically in one hemisphere of the brain via stereotactic AAV injections was shown to lead to Tomato expression in both the ipsilateral and contralateral epididymis (Figure 2), arguing against short-range neuronal delivery
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the AAV injection studies.

claim: Parabiosis and serum transfer studies support the hypothesis that Cre activity synthesized in a variety of tissues can access the circulation and subsequently be trafficked to the male reproductive tract.
source: Indeed, our follow-up studies using parabioses and serum transfers support the hypothesis that Cre activity synthesized in a variety of tissues can access the circulation and subsequently be trafficked to the male reproductive tract.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the parabiosis and serum transfer experimental data.

claim: The circulating Cre activity likely consists of Cre mRNA, rather than protein.
source: We speculate that the circulating Cre activity consists of Cre mRNA, rather than protein
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and precedent in the literature.

claim: The RNA is anticipated to be present either in exosomes or in ribonucleoprotein complexes protected from serum nucleases.
source: and we anticipate that the RNA is present either in exosomes or in ribonucleoprotein complexes protected from serum nucleases.
evidence: This is speculation based on known mechanisms of RNA stability in circulation.

claim: Cre mRNA can be documented by PCR in the circulation of multiple Cre lines.
source: Indeed, we can document Cre mRNA by PCR in the circulation of multiple Cre lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated through RT-PCR analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: There is abundant precedent for RNA transmission between different tissues.
source: and there is abundant precedent for RNA transmission between different tissues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In C. elegans, introduction of double stranded RNA either by injection or by feeding with dsRNA-expressing bacteria leads to organism-wide silencing of homologous genes.
source: For instance, in Caenorhabditis elegans, introduction of double stranded RNA either by injection or by feeding with dsRNA-expressing bacteria leads to organism-wide silencing of homologous genes (Fire et al., 1998; Timmons and Fire, 1998)
evidence: This is based on cited literature on systemic RNAi in C. elegans.

claim: Expression of RNAi triggers in neurons has been shown to silence target genes in the germline in C. elegans.
source: Moreover, expression of RNAi triggers in neurons has been shown to silence target genes in the germline (Devanapally et al., 2015)
evidence: This is based on cited literature on neuron-to-germline RNA trafficking in C. elegans.

claim: Systemic RNA trafficking is well described in plants, as various means of introducing dsRNA into aerial tissues can drive sequence-specific silencing in roots.
source: Systemic RNA trafficking is also well described in plants, as various means of introducing dsRNA into aerial tissues can drive sequence-specific silencing in roots (Palauqui et al., 1997; Voinnet et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on systemic RNA trafficking in plants.

claim: In mammals, many studies have reported RNA or protein trafficking between different cell types within the same tissue.
source: In mammals, many studies have reported RNA or protein trafficking between different cell types within the same tissue (van Niel et al., 2018)
evidence: This is based on cited literature on inter-cellular trafficking in mammals.

claim: RNA or protein trafficking between distant tissues has been reported in mammals.
source: or between distant tissues (Thomou et al., 2017; Poggio et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on inter-tissue trafficking in mammals.

claim: There are only sporadic reports of RNA trafficking from distant tissues to germ cells themselves in mammals.
source: Although this is well documented for several somatic tissues, in the unique case of the germline there are only sporadic reports of RNA trafficking from distant tissues to germ cells themselves (Cossetti et al., 2014; O'Brien et al., 2020; Conine and Rando, 2022).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on RNA trafficking to the germline in mammals.

claim: Gametogenesis is supported by a wide variety of somatic cells and accessory tissues that could serve as intermediaries between distal tissues and developing gametes.
source: That said, it is worth noting that gametogenesis is supported by a wide variety of somatic cells and accessory tissues, and these could serve as intermediaries between distal tissues and developing gametes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of reproductive biology.

claim: The epididymis is a tissue where sperm mature for approximately 1-2 weeks following the completion of testicular development.
source: In our efforts to explore the biology of the male reproductive tract, we unexpectedly found that expression of Cre in the central nervous system resulted in recombination in the epididymis, a tissue where sperm mature for ~1–2 weeks following the completion of testicular development.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of epididymal biology.

claim: Zeybel et al. reported that repeated serum transfers from CCl4-treated animals to a recipient were sufficient to reproduce H3K27me3 changes in the sperm of the recipient animal.
source: First, in their studies of intergenerational effects of carbon tetrachloride, Zeybel et al. reported that repeated serum transfers from CCl4-treated animals to a recipient were sufficient to reproduce H3K27me3 changes in the sperm of the recipient animal (Zeybel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on serum transfer effects on sperm epigenetics.

claim: Mansuy and colleagues reported that transferring serum from males subject to early life stress to a recipient male was sufficient to drive altered glucose responses in the F1 offspring of the recipient animal.
source: More recently, Mansuy and colleagues reported that transferring serum from males subject to early life stress to a recipient male was sufficient to drive altered glucose responses in the F1 offspring of the recipient animal (van Steenwyk et al., 2020)
evidence: This is based on cited literature on serum transfer effects on offspring phenotypes.

claim: A prior report in mouse suggested that microRNAs expressed in the brain could be delivered to sperm, and subsequently to the next generation.
source: Intriguingly, a prior report in mouse suggested that microRNAs expressed in the brain could be delivered to sperm, and subsequently to the next generation (O'Brien et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on brain-to-sperm RNA trafficking.

claim: With the exception of Syn1 and Nestin, there is no evidence for neuronal Cre trafficking directly to sperm cells.
source: However, with the exception of Syn1 and Nestin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we do not find any evidence for neuronal Cre trafficking directly to sperm cells
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the imaging data.

claim: Even in the case of Syn1 and Nestin Cre drivers, recombination in the germline likely occurs prior to the last stages of spermatogenesis in the testis.
source: Even in the case of Syn1 and Nestin Cre drivers, recombination in the germline likely occurs prior to the last stages of spermatogenesis in the testis – potentially in spermatogonial stem cells or even earlier in development – and not during epididymal transit.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of Tomato expression observed.

claim: The data place the epididymis as a mediator between neuronal information processing and programming of the sperm epigenome.
source: Our data instead would place the epididymis as a mediator between neuronal information processing and programming of the sperm epigenome
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: CNS-derived information potentially drives altered epididymal physiology and consequent remodeling of sperm small RNAs, proteins, or surface lipids.
source: with CNS-derived information potentially driving altered epididymal physiology and consequent remodeling of sperm small RNAs, proteins, or surface lipids.
evidence: This is speculation about potential biological implications of the findings.

claim: Different Cre drivers result in recombination in different parts of the epididymis, arguing for some level of specificity between different tissue-derived exosomes and target cell populations in the epididymis.
source: We disfavor this model, in part because different Cre drivers result in recombination in different parts of the epididymis, arguing for some level of specificity between different tissue-derived exosomes (for instance) and target cell populations in the epididymis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential patterns of recombination observed.
